# Sparse and Efficient Representations

Also called: Sparse NeRF, Local NeRF, Decomposed NeRF

## Overview
This family addresses the prohibitive memory and computational costs of dense [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRFs) in large-scale or high-resolution scenes by decomposing the global radiance field into localized, sparse components [S1]. Unlike dense representations that query a single global network for every point, these methods partition space or features to enable parallel training, reduce per-point latency, and allow for efficient mesh extraction [S1, S2, S3]. They distinguish themselves from sibling architectures like [AdaNeRF](6195-adanerf.md) or [Transformer-based Architectures](8998-transformer-based-architectures.md) by explicitly leveraging spatial sparsity or [hierarchical decomposition](#827-hierarchical-vector-quantization.md) rather than adaptive feature hashing or attention mechanisms alone.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family compute a radiance field function $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d})$ that outputs volume density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ for a query point $\mathbf{x}$ and direction $\mathbf{d}$. The final pixel color $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})$ for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ is computed via the [standard volume rendering](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md) integral:
$$
\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T_i \alpha_i \mathbf{c}_i
$$
where $\alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)$ and $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$. The architectural variations lie in how $\sigma_i$ and $\mathbf{c}_i$ are generated from the input coordinates, how the network is structured (depth, width, connectivity), and what auxiliary inputs (embeddings, priors, features) are fused into the computation.

## Subtopics

### [Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning](8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md)
Decomposes a large-scale scene into spatial cells, each managed by a separate MLP submodule, to enable parallel training and reduce memory usage. It distinguishes itself from dense NeRFs by using spatial locality to limit the training data assigned to each network, and from other sparse methods by employing a fixed 2D grid tessellation for centroid selection rather than dynamic clustering.

### [Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation](8876-sparse-radiance-field-srf-representation.md)
A voxel-based representation of a 3D scene or object that stores density and view-dependent radiance colors in a sparse grid structure. It serves as a compact, differentiable alternative to dense neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and dense [voxel grids](#1719-voxel-grid-indexing.md), enabling efficient optimization and rendering by storing data only for occupied regions. Unlike its siblings, [Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning](#8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md) and [KiloNeRF](#8942-kilonerf.md), which use hierarchical or [tree-based structures](#4139-tree-based-structures-octree-pointer-tree-sparse-voxel-dag.md) for scalability, SRF relies on a flat, coordinate-based (COO) sparse array, making mesh extraction straightforward via Marching Cubes.

### [KiloNeRF](8942-kilonerf.md)
KiloNeRF is a sparse and efficient representation method that decomposes a large, deep [Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) into a set of small, shallow MLPs arranged in a 3D grid. It solves the problem of high per-point computational cost in [standard NeRFs](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) by using a teacher-student training paradigm to distill knowledge into lightweight local models. It sets itself apart from siblings like Mega-NeRF by focusing on reducing the computational cost per sample via tiny MLPs rather than just spatial partitioning for ray traversal, and from SRF by using explicit MLPs per cell rather than feature vectors.

## Background
The primary motivation for sparse and efficient representations is the $O(N)$ memory and compute complexity of dense NeRFs, which scales poorly with scene size and resolution. Early works like [KiloNeRF](8942-kilonerf.md) and [Mega-NeRF](8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md) introduced spatial [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) to enable training on large-scale datasets (e.g., OpenImages, Mapillary) that exceed GPU memory limits [S1]. [Sparse Radiance Fields (SRF)](8876-sparse-radiance-field-srf-representation.md) further optimized this by using [sparse voxel grids](#8430-sparse-spatial-data-structures-for-nerf.md) to reduce storage and accelerate rendering through direct memory access, facilitating real-time applications and mesh extraction [S1]. These methods form the foundation for modern large-scale [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) [training pipelines](#5325-training-pipeline.md).
